title: Phaedrus: Socrates on divine madness, the winged soul, and the true art of speech
summary: In Plato's Phaedrus Socrates first mocks a clever speech against love, then recants with a myth of the soul as a charioteer with two horses, showing love as a divine madness that regrows the soul's wings. He then argues that real rhetoric needs knowledge of truth and of souls, and that the living word in the soul beats writing.

principles.text: Know yourself before chasing curiosities about myths and monsters.
principles.quote: I must first know myself, as the Delphian inscription says; to be curious about that which is not my concern, while I am still in ignorance of my own self, would be ridiculous.

principles.text: Not all madness is an evil: some is a divine gift and the source of great blessings.
principles.quote: there is also a madness which is a divine gift, and the source of the chiefest blessings granted to men.

principles.text: The soul is immortal because it is self-moving and the source of all motion.
principles.quote: Only the self-moving, never leaving self, never ceases to move, and is the fountain and beginning of motion to all that moves besides.

principles.text: The soul is like a charioteer driving a noble horse and an unruly one; self-mastery lets reason and shame tame desire.
principles.quote: if the better elements of the mind which lead to order and philosophy prevail, then they pass their life here in happiness and harmony-masters of themselves and orderly-enslaving the vicious and emancipating the virtuous elements of the soul

principles.text: A speaker must know the truth of his subject; persuasion without knowledge of good and evil is harmful.
principles.quote: He, then, who being ignorant of the truth aims at appearances, will only attain an art of rhetoric which is ridiculous and is not an art at all?

principles.text: Good method means gathering scattered particulars into one idea, then dividing by natural joints.
principles.quote: First, the comprehension of scattered particulars in one idea; ... The second principle is that of division into species according to the natural formation, where the joint is, not breaking any part as a bad carver might.
